summary: Defines conferencing call control features for SIP, building on the conferencing requirements and framework documents. It describes how a tightly coupled SIP conference works from the perspective of different user agent types. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: This document explains how a conference call works in SIP. One server, called the focus, runs the meeting and talks to each participant separately. A participant joins by dialling the conference address, and asks the focus to invite or remove others using a REFER request.

subtitle: How SIP user agents join, leave and are moved in and out of a conference call.

tldr.problem: SIP can set up a two-party call, but a conference needs a central point that decides who is in it, and needs a way for one participant to pull another one in or push one out.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines how a focus, the server that runs the conference, and its participants exchange ordinary SIP messages. Joining is an INVITE to the conference address, and adding or removing someone is a REFER.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Best Current Practice, BCP 119, published in August 2006. It is built only from plain SIP, so a participant that knows nothing about conferencing can still take part.

facts.label: Joining a conference
facts.value: INVITE with the Request-URI set to the conference URI

facts.label: Adding a participant
facts.value: REFER with a Refer-To header field

facts.label: Conference state updates

sections.title: What This Document Adds to SIP Conferencing
sections.content:
The specification uses the concepts and definitions from the high level requirements document and the SIP conferencing framework document, and is applicable to tightly coupled SIP conferences. In this architecture a user agent, known as a participant, establishes a SIP dialog with another user agent, known as a focus. The focus is the central point of control, authentication and authorization. The document defines the operation of a focus and of participant user agents. Only the signalling needs to be centralized in this model; the media can be centrally mixed, distributed, or even multicast.

The approach implements key functions in the conferencing framework using SIP primitives only, which allows simple conferences with defined functionalities to be conducted using SIP mechanisms and conventions. Many other advanced functions can be implemented using additional means, but they are not in the scope of this document. The call control and dialog manipulation approach is based on the multiparty framework document, which defines the basic approach of service design adopted for SIP: definition of primitives, not services; a signalling model independent of the service; an invoker-oriented approach; primitives that make full use of URIs; policies for authentication, authorization and logging; and graceful fallback to baseline SIP.

The use of opaque URIs and the ability to communicate call control context information within a URI, as opposed to using service-related header fields, is fundamental to this approach. The document presents the basic call control building blocks for dial-in and dial-out conferencing from the user agent perspective, and possible applications include ad-hoc conferences and scheduled conferences. A single conference can bridge participants with different capabilities who have joined by different means.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP is built for two-party calls. A conference needs someone in charge, and this document works out how to build that using only the SIP messages that already exist.

sections.title: The Focus and the Three Kinds of User Agent
sections.content:
A focus hosts a SIP conference and maintains a SIP signalling relationship with each participant in the conference. A focus contains a conference-aware user agent that supports the conferencing call control conventions defined in this document. A focus SHOULD support the conference package of RFC 4575, behave as a notifier for that package, and indicate its support in the Allow-Events header fields in requests and responses. A focus MAY include information about the conference in SDP bodies sent as part of normal SIP signalling by populating the Session Information, URI, Email Address and Phone Number SDP fields. To support advanced features, where a session established between two endpoints can migrate to a centralized conference, a focus SHOULD support the Replaces header field. A user agent with focus capabilities could be implemented in end user equipment and used for the creation of ad-hoc conferences, and a dedicated conferencing server whose primary task is to simultaneously host conferences of arbitrary type and size may allocate and publish a conference factory URI for creating an arbitrary number of ad-hoc conferences, and subsequently their focuses, using SIP call control means. A successful attempt to establish a call to this URI results in the automatic creation of a new conference and its focus, and the Conference Factory URI and the newly created focus URI MAY resolve to different physical devices.

A conference-unaware user agent is the simplest: it can participate in a conference ignoring all SIP conferencing-related information, and can dial in to a conference and be invited to one. It need only support RFC 3261, and conferencing information is optionally conveyed to or from it using non-SIP means. The presence of an isfocus feature tag in a Contact header field will not cause interoperability problems with such an agent, since it is treated as an unknown header parameter and ignored, as per standard SIP behaviour.

A conference-aware user agent supports the conferencing call control conventions defined in this document as a conference participant, in addition to support of RFC 3261, and should be able to process SIP redirections. It MUST recognise the isfocus feature parameter, and SHOULD support REFER, SIP events and the conferencing package. It SHOULD subscribe to the conference package if the isfocus parameter is in the remote target URI of a dialog and the conference package is listed by a focus in an Allow-Events header field. The SUBSCRIBE to the conference package SHOULD be sent outside any INVITE-initiated dialog, and termination of the INVITE dialog with a BYE does not necessarily terminate the SUBSCRIBE dialog.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds of program here. The focus runs the meeting. A conference-aware participant understands the extra rules. A conference-unaware participant just takes part, and even it does not need to change.

sections.title: The isfocus Feature Parameter
sections.content:
The main design guidelines for the development of SIP extensions and conventions for conferencing are to define the minimum number of extensions and to have seamless backward compatibility with conference-unaware SIP user agents. The minimal requirement for SIP is being able to express that a dialog is part of a certain conference referenced by a URI. As a result it is possible to create a conference, join a conference, invite a user to a conference, expel a user by a third party, discover if a URI is a conference URI, and delete a conference.

The approach taken is to use the feature parameter isfocus to express that a SIP dialog belongs to a conference. In session establishment a focus MUST include the isfocus feature parameter in the Contact header field unless the focus wishes to hide the fact that it is a focus. To a participant the feature parameter is associated with the remote target URI of the dialog, and it indicates that the resulting dialog belongs to a conference, identified by the URI in the Contact header field, and that the call control conventions defined in this document can be applied.

By their nature the conferences supported by this specification are centralized, so a conferencing system typically needs to allocate a SIP conference URI such that SIP requests to it are not forked and are routed to a dedicated conference focus. A globally accessible SIP conference could be well constructed with a conference URI using a Globally Routable User Agent URI, because of its ability to support the non-forking and global routability requirements.

Discovery is implemented with an OPTIONS request, inside an active dialog or outside one. A focus MUST include the isfocus feature parameter in a 200 OK response to an OPTIONS unless the focus wishes to hide the fact that it is a focus. The response also carries the Allow, Accept, Allow-Events and Supported header fields, which tell the caller which methods, body types, event packages and extensions the focus supports.
sections.plainLanguage: One extra tag in the Contact header says that the other end is running a conference and gives the conference's address. A participant can also ask that question directly with an OPTIONS request.

sections.title: Joining a Conference by Dialling In
sections.content:
In this scenario a user knows the conference URI and dials in to join the conference. The focus authenticates the participant and applies authorization policy before allowing the participant to join. If the user agent is the first participant of the conference to dial in, it is likely that this INVITE will activate the focus and hence the conference, although the conference URI must have been reserved prior to its use. If the conference is already running, the dialling-in participant is joined to the conference by its focus.

To join an existing specific conference, a user agent sends an INVITE with the Request-URI set to the conference URI, and the focus MUST include the isfocus feature parameter in the Contact header field of the 200 OK response to the INVITE. A conference-aware participant that sees the parameter knows it is in a conference and that the conferencing conventions apply, and it may then subscribe to the conference package so that it learns about participants joining and leaving. A conference-unaware participant simply treats the call as an ordinary SIP call.
sections.plainLanguage: Joining is an ordinary call to the conference's address. The server answers in the normal way, with one extra tag that tells a smart participant what kind of call this is.

sections.title: Adding and Removing Participants with REFER
sections.content:
The REFER method is the main tool for pulling other people into a conference and for pushing them out of it. A participant may request that the focus add a new resource to a conference by sending a REFER to the focus, and the focus then issues an INVITE to that participant's URI. The REFER is answered with a 202 Accepted, and the outcome is reported back to the requesting participant with NOTIFY requests, first reporting the attempt and then the final result.

A participant may also ask the focus to refer a participant to dial in to the conference. In that case the Refer-To header field has its method set to REFER and contains an escaped Refer-To header field holding the conference URI, so that the participant being referred is told to call the conference itself. Asking for a participant to be removed from a conference uses REFER with a BYE method in the Refer-To header field, so that the focus sends the BYE on the participant's behalf.

The document sets out these flows with example call flow diagrams, and covers the equivalent scenarios in which a conference is created manually by dialling in to a conferencing application, and in which an ad-hoc conference is created using ad-hoc SIP methods.
sections.plainLanguage: To invite someone, a participant sends a REFER to the conference server, which then calls the guest. To remove someone, the same message is used with a BYE inside it, and the server sends the hang-up.

sections.title: Switching Devices and Moving a Call into a Conference
sections.content:
Two header fields let a participant change the session it is in. The Join header field is used when dialling in to a conference using a third-party dialog identifier, and the Replaces header field is used when switching user agents within a conference and when transferring a point-to-point session into a conference.

The transfer flow works like this. Alice and Bob have an established session with a dialog identifier A-B. Alice joins the conference with the focus by sending an INVITE to the conference URI, and then sends a REFER request to the focus asking it to send an INVITE request to the other participant. Alice includes an escaped Replaces header field in the URI included in the Refer-To header field. Bob receives the INVITE from the focus and matches the dialog in the Replaces header field with the dialog with Alice, so Bob accepts the INVITE, joins the conference, and sends a BYE to Alice to tear down their point-to-point dialog.

A single conference can bridge participants that have different capabilities and who have joined by different means, and a focus is expected to support the Replaces header field so that a session established between two endpoints can migrate to a centralized conference.
sections.plainLanguage: Two participants talking to each other can be pulled into a conference without either of them dialling again: one asks the conference server to call the other, and a header field tells the second participant which call to replace.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This specification defines the interaction between a focus and a participant in a conferencing application, so the security considerations and mechanisms defined in RFC 3261 apply, and there are some aspects unique to conferencing. A conference often involves substantial network bandwidth and computing resources, so authentication is even more important than in a simple peer-to-peer session. Conferences often have policy related to conferencing resources, and a focus SHOULD authenticate participants before joining them to a conference and allowing use of conferencing resources, applying different policies to different participants based on the result of the authentication. A participant, on the other hand, is interacting with a number of other participants through the focus, so it should authenticate the focus and be sure that the focus used for the conference is trusted. Normal SIP authentication mechanisms are suitable, such as SIP Digest with a shared secret, certificates, or a secured SIP identity mechanism, and a focus SHOULD support Secure SIP connections so that hop-by-hop mutual authentication and confidentiality provided by TLS can be achieved.

Because the focus uses the isfocus feature tag to indicate that it is acting as a focus, header fields such as Contact SHOULD have end to end integrity, and a participant and focus SHOULD support an end-to-end integrity mechanism such as S/MIME. Once a participant has learned that the other user agent is a focus, call control operations such as REFER can be implemented, and the security considerations of RFC 3515 apply to any such operation. A focus accepting subscriptions to the conference package must follow the security considerations in RFC 4575: since notifications can carry sensitive information, the subscriptions should be authenticated and the notifications delivered with confidentiality and integrity protection, and since a participant cannot authenticate other participants directly, it must rely on the focus to do so. A focus MUST support a participant's request for privacy, either through conference policy or as expressed through the signalling. For example, a participant joining a conference and including a Privacy header field must not have identity information revealed to other participants by the focus.
sections.plainLanguage: A conference server has to check who is let in, and participants have to check that the server really is the server and not someone in the middle. Both ends should encrypt what they say, and a participant who asks not to be named must not be named to the others.

viz.caption: THE THREE KINDS OF SIP USER AGENT IN A CONFERENCE

items.title: Focus
items.text: Runs the conference. Holds a separate dialogue with each participant and decides who is admitted.

items.title: Conference-aware UA
items.text: Understands the isfocus tag, supports REFER and SIP events, and can subscribe to the conference package.

items.title: Conference-unaware UA
items.text: Takes part in the call without understanding conferencing at all. It ignores the extra tag and needs no changes.
